title: Sort parts off a belt that stops dead, surges to double speed and has a part shoved aside mid-run
instruction: Sort the cubes riding on the belt before they go into the tunnel: red cubes in the red bin, blue cubes in the blue bin. The belt changes speed without warning.
context: Real lines don't run at one speed: a jam downstream stops the belt, it then runs fast to clear the backlog, and parts get knocked out of place on the way. Whoever sorts at the line must notice each change as it happens and re-aim at where each part is now, not where it was going to be. Done by: line operators, sorters and pick-and-place cells on packing and recycling lines.
setup: The two arm bases stand 61 cm apart on an oak table (1.10 x 1.30 m) whose edges are 65 cm either side of the midpoint between the bases. A straight conveyor crosses the table parallel to the line through the bases, its centre line 34 cm in front of them, flowing from the robot's right to its left. It runs from 66.5 cm right to 90 cm left of the midpoint: its right end overhangs the table by 1.5 cm, and past the table's left edge its tunnel stands on a dark steel post to the floor (18.5 x 4 cm, centred 87 cm left of the midpoint). Two dark steel rails (1.5 x 1.5 cm, 156.5 cm long) run along it, centred 4 cm either side of the centre line. Four grey steel carrier plates (14 cm across the belt, 9 cm along it, 1.5 cm thick) ride 2 mm above the rails, square to them, centred on the centre line; nose to tail 11 cm apart (centre to centre); at the start their centres are 28, 39, 50 and 61 cm right of the midpoint. Each carrier has one painted wooden cube (4 cm, 50 g) in its middle, square to it: from the front of the line (the leftmost) blue, red, blue, red. From 42 cm left of the midpoint the conveyor runs into a grey sheet-steel tunnel: two side walls (1 cm thick, 9.2 cm tall, 48 cm long) whose inner faces are 8.25 cm either side of the centre line, under a 0.8 cm roof whose underside is 2 cm above the cubes' tops, closed at its far end (90 cm left of the midpoint). Behind the belt, centred 8 cm left of the midpoint, a dark steel guide block (20 x 8 cm, 3.3 cm tall) stands on the table from 44 to 64 cm in front of the bases, and on it lies a flat grey steel pusher bar (22 cm long toward the robot, 6 cm wide, 1 cm thick, its underside 3 mm above the carriers' tops) whose front face is 8.5 cm behind the belt's centre line (1.5 cm behind the carriers). A red plastic bin and a blue plastic bin (16 x 16 cm outside, 14 x 14 cm inside, 1 cm floor, 5 cm walls) stand square on the table, their centres 14 cm in front of the bases (their far walls 5 cm from the carriers), the red one 30 cm right and the blue one 30 cm left of the midpoint (in front of the right and the left arm). The belt's run, from the start of the trial (every change of speed takes 0.3 s, smoothly): 4 cm/s from 0 s; stop at 9 s; 8 cm/s from 14.5 s; 4 cm/s from 19.5 s; stop at 28.5 s, when every carrier is inside the tunnel. While the belt stands still the first blue cube is in front of the pusher bar; the bar moves 10.5 cm toward the robot in 0.8 s from 9.4 s (shoving that cube 4 cm across its carrier, toward the robot), stays 0.1 s and goes back in 0.6 s, at rest again from 10.9 s.
scoring: At the end of the trial: 0.25 for each cube lying in the bin of its own colour, minus 0.25 for each cube lying in the other bin, never below 0. A cube is in a bin when its centre is between the bin's inner walls and below the top of its walls, and it is still. A cube anywhere else (still on a carrier, gone into the tunnel, on the table or floor, held in a gripper) counts 0. So 1.0 when all four are in their own bins (the trial then ends with success once this has held for 1 s); 0.75, 0.5 or 0.25 for three, two or one, less 0.25 for every cube in the wrong bin; 0 for nothing sorted, for every cube in one bin, or for more wrong than right.
reset_notes: Run the carriers back to their start positions, put each cube back square in the middle of its carrier, return the pusher bar, and start the belt's schedule with the trial. Every cube that went into the tunnel is still on its carrier there.
fidelity: The carriers and pusher bar follow their paths exactly, like servo-driven axes: the arms can't push or stop them, where a real line would stop on a jam. Carriers ride 2 mm above the rails; the bar's drive (an air cylinder on a real line) is not modelled. The cubes have the station's rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), more than painted wood on steel; at the belt's peak 0.42 m/s² they don't slide, and the bar pushes only their lowest 1.3 cm, too low to tip them.
